updates.alert: I'm not trading this time, and I'm keeping every position close to its current weight so I don't pay commissions for nothing. Most of the portfolio rose this week: Targa +12.6%, Marathon +10.4%, Valero +9.7%, Keysight +9.6% and CrowdStrike +6.1%. Keysight and NetApp both report soon, so selling them into results would lock in losses just as the tech selloff may be easing. Illumina has its Jefferies conference talk on November 17. Fortinet is my biggest loser at -24%, but at about 5% of the portfolio it's a small position, and I'd rather judge it on news than on price alone. I'm watching three risks: refiner margins (Marathon and Valero), a renewed slide in tech hardware (Keysight and NetApp), and a reversal in health care after a strong three months (Merck, Viatris, Humana).
updates.market_view: Stocks bounced this week: the S&P 500 rose 2.3% but is still down 2.5% over the past month. The rebound was broad, led by utilities, consumer stocks, financials and industrials. Tech is still the weak spot, down 6.9% over the month and 8.5% over three months. The hardest-hit chip and hardware stocks bounced sharply, but this looks like a relief rally inside a selloff, not a clean trend change.
updates.self_review: Holding everything on Wednesday worked out: refiners, Targa, Keysight and CrowdStrike rebounded strongly, and the portfolio avoided commissions. Fortinet and Illumina are still the weak spots I need to keep an eye on.

updates.alert: I'm not making any trades this week. Illumina is down 21% in a month, but that drop followed a third quarter that beat estimates and raised full-year guidance. The selling looks like profit-taking after a big run, not damage to the business, so I'm holding it at under 5% ahead of its Jefferies conference talk on November 17. Keysight and NetApp both report in the next couple of weeks; Keysight is expected around November 23, though the date isn't confirmed. Keysight rose 7% last week, and I don't want to pay commissions to sell either name just before results that could reverse the tech selloff. The portfolio's 2026 gains are already spread across health care (Merck, Humana, Viatris), materials (Nucor, DuPont) and energy pipelines (Targa), which offset the tech weakness. The main risks I'm watching are further falls in refiner profit margins (Marathon and Valero), more forced selling in cybersecurity and storage stocks, and a disappointing Keysight report.
updates.market_view: The S&P 500 slipped again this week (-1.0%) and is down 2.3% over a month. updates.self_review: Humana is up 4% since I bought it and helped cushion the portfolio during a week when the market fell. Holding Fortinet instead of selling it at the bottom was neutral: the stock was roughly flat for the week (-0.6%).

updates.alert: I'm not selling anything this week. I'm adding a new position in Humana at about 5%, paid for from cash. Fortinet's stock is down 37% in a month, but its third quarter was strong: revenue grew 20% and it raised full-year billings guidance for the third time this year, so I'm keeping it rather than selling at the bottom of an AI-driven tech selloff. Humana rose about 15% in October after its 2027 Medicare star ratings improved sharply. That reverses the ratings problem that hurt its 2026 earnings, and the stock moves less than most of what I hold. The portfolio leans heavily on energy and on tech that tends to swing more than the market, so a health insurer whose recovery doesn't depend on oil prices or AI spending improves the balance. The main risks I'm watching are a further fall in refiner profit margins, more forced selling in tech before Keysight and NetApp report, and Medicare cost trends for Humana.
updates.market_view: Tech is being sold hard: the AI-linked hardware and semiconductor names are down 17-50% in a month, while health care, staples and consumer stocks are rising. Energy also gave back gains this week as refiners and midstream fell together, and the S&P 500 is down 5% over the month. This looks like money moving out of crowded AI winners and into defensive names, not a broad collapse: 56% of members are still above their 200-day average.
updates.self_review: Since October 19 the portfolio is down about 8.6%, versus roughly 5% for the S&P 500 over the past month. Holding many tech and refiner momentum names left it exposed to the tech-hardware selloff and the drop in refiners; Merck, DuPont and Viatris helped but couldn't offset it. Not trading on Wednesday avoided costs, but the portfolio still leans too heavily on high-volatility names, which this small defensive addition starts to fix.

new.thesis: Much better 2027 Medicare star ratings support earnings recovering from the depressed 2026 base by 2028; a defensive name that doesn't depend on oil prices or AI spending.

updates.alert: I'm not making any real trades this week. The only change is trimming Merck from 10.7% back to the 10% cap. Marathon Petroleum fell 12% even though it reported adjusted earnings of $26.93 a share, ahead of the roughly $25 expected, and raised its dividend 10%. I read the drop as a sign that refiner profit margins are near their peak, not as a broken story, so I'm keeping both refiners. Illumina dropped after third-quarter revenue missed, but it raised its full-year revenue and earnings forecasts and free cash flow grew strongly. Keysight's slide came without any company news; it was caught in the AI-linked tech selloff, and it reports in mid-to-late November. The candidates are mostly falling chip and hardware stocks or high-flyers like Moderna, and none is clearly enough better than what I hold to justify the costs and the tax hit of switching. My main risks are falling refiner margins, the tech selloff continuing into Fortinet, Keysight and NetApp, and how much of the portfolio sits in energy.
updates.market_view: Investors are swapping out of technology and into defensive and cyclical value. Tech fell 13% in the past month while health care, staples, financials and materials each rose about 9-13%. The S&P 500 is roughly flat over 3 months and 67% of its members are still above their 200-day average, so this looks like a rotation driven by AI-linked selling rather than a broad bear market.
updates.self_review: Keeping Fortinet last week was roughly neutral (+1%). The broad tech and energy selloff hurt Keysight (-15%), NetApp (-16%), Marathon (-12%) and Illumina (-22%), while Merck, DuPont and Viatris gained. The portfolio has fallen behind the S&P 500 since starting, mainly because so much of it is in tech and energy.

updates.alert: I'm making no real trades this week. The only change is a small trim of Merck from 10.4% back to the 10% cap, because the stock's gain pushed it over the limit. Fortinet is down about 21% from my cost after its October 28 report, but revenue grew 20%, billings grew 29% and guidance went up. Selling a better business after it has already been marked down would just lock in the loss. This week's candidates are utilities (AES, Ameren) and insurers (Aflac, AIG) that have already rallied about 10% in a month. They are slow-growth, and none is clearly better than what I hold by enough to pay the trading costs. The risks I'm watching are refiner profit margins (Marathon and Valero), the market's habit of selling good earnings reports in tech (Fortinet, Keysight, NetApp), and Illumina's weak price trend.
updates.market_view: The market went nowhere this week: the S&P 500 ETF was +0.1% over both one week and one month, and +1.2% over three months. Breadth still looks healthy, with about 80% of measured members above their 200-day average. Financials (+9.5% over the month) and utilities (+5.4%) led, which hints at a move toward safer stocks while the market keeps punishing good earnings reports from expensive growth names.
updates.self_review: Making no trades last week was right for most holdings: CRWD, DD, TRGP and MS are all up. The Fortinet drop stung, but it was driven by worries about the future, not a miss on the numbers, so I'm still holding the position.

updates.alert: I'm making no trades again this week. The big news is Fortinet, down about 26% after its third-quarter report on October 28. Revenue grew 20%, billings grew 29%, earnings beat estimates and the company raised its full-year guidance. Investors seem worried that the firewall upgrade wave is close to its peak, that service revenue will come in later than hoped, and that the stock was too expensive. I don't think selling the day after the drop makes sense when the business numbers got better. At about 36 times this year's guided earnings, though, it isn't cheap enough for me to buy more, so I'm keeping it at its now-smaller 5% weight. Valero earned $23.90 a share in the quarter on near-record refinery use, yet the stock still fell 10%. That looks like profit-taking, not a broken thesis. The risks I'm watching are the market's selling of good earnings reports, refiner profit margins (energy is still about 23% of the portfolio), Keysight and Morgan Stanley, which are still weak, and Merck's results.
updates.market_view: The S&P 500 went nowhere this week (-0.3%), but the moves underneath it were sharp. Energy, utilities, staples and health care led over the past month, while communication services lagged and last quarter's semiconductor and hardware winners pulled back hard: names like STX, LRCX, AMAT and TER are 20-40% off their highs. Earnings season is punishing stocks priced for perfection even when results are good, so I'd rather not chase price swings right now.
updates.self_review: Holding everything last week was mostly right: CrowdStrike, DuPont, NetApp, Nucor and Targa all gained. Fortinet's post-earnings collapse took most of the gain away. That loss came from one stock-specific risk, which spreading the money over 13 names was supposed to absorb, and it did.

updates.alert: This is the first decision, so I'm putting about 90% of the $10,000 into 13 stocks and holding 10% in cash. The biggest positions are Merck, Marathon Petroleum, Targa Resources and Nucor. Each has strong 12-month gains and kept rising or held steady this week while the rest of the market fell. I'm buying cybersecurity (CrowdStrike, Fortinet) and storage (NetApp) after their 13-17% drops this week. Their trends are intact, and buying now means entering below their recent highs. I'm deliberately skipping the most extreme momentum names, Moderna (+732% in 12 months), Lumentum and Bloom Energy, because their daily price swings are too wild to size sensibly. The main risks I'm watching: refining margins could fall back, the AI and tech selling could spread to my software names, and a broader pullback could hit Morgan Stanley through weaker capital-markets activity. These are judgments from the brief's price data only; I didn't run any news searches this week.
updates.market_view: The S&P 500 fell 2.1% this week and is flat over the last month. Only about half its members trade above their 200-day average, so the market's strength is narrow. This week's selling hit the AI and hardware names hard: Lumentum, Dell, HPE and Coherent each fell 20-25%. Leadership has moved to energy, especially refiners, and to health care, while communication services keep falling. I'm building a diversified portfolio weighted toward steadier momentum: refiners, pipelines, pharma, steel and cybersecurity. I'm keeping 10% cash because the market is fragile.

new.thesis: Large pharma with +74% 12-1 month momentum, low volatility and a strong balance sheet. Health care is the best defensive sector this quarter (+12.5% over 3 months).
Leading refiner trading only 1% under its 52-week high, up 13% this month and 49% over 3 months as refining margins widen. Large share buybacks support the stock.

A second refiner that benefits from the same margin conditions, with steady operations and strong cash returns to shareholders. I'm holding it smaller than MPC to limit how much I depend on one industry.
Pipeline company earning fee-based income from growing natural-gas volumes. It has near-high momentum (+91% 12-1 month) with only moderate volatility.
Steelmaker with +93% 12-1 month momentum and low volatility for its sector, helped by tariff protection and a conservative balance sheet.
Leader in endpoint security with growing recurring revenue. After this week's 17% drop it is a chance to buy a strong +102% 12-1 month trend that is still well above its 200-day average.
Security company with good profitability and a firewall upgrade cycle, now 13% under its high after this week's drop.
Storage company with a cheaper valuation than other AI hardware, benefiting from demand for flash storage in data centers. It is +23% over 3 months even after this week's pullback.
Test-and-measurement company with improving orders across AI, wireless and defense customers, and +104% 12-1 month momentum.
Leader in gene sequencing whose results are recovering. The stock is +36% over 3 months and 54% above its 200-day average.
Cheap generic-drug maker at a fresh 52-week high, with debt coming down and cash going back to shareholders.
DuPont after its split, now a more focused company in electronics and water. The stock is up 69% in 12 months and has moved only modestly in the past month, a calm way to own industrial exposure.
Wealth-management franchise whose stock is 21% off its high. I'm making it a small position to add financials at a lower price.
